PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

A conjunction is a joining word. In this sub-strand you will find the coordinating conjunctions and, but, or, yet, so, for and nor in talk and writing about hygiene and sanitation. You will use them in short dialogues and in your own sentences so that your ideas fit together clearly.

## Strand 10.0: Hygiene and Sanitation
Sub-strand 10.3.1: Grammar in Use: Word Class (Conjunctions)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify conjunctions correctly in oral and written texts for fluency in speech
b) engage in short dialogues featuring conjunctions for fluency in speech
c) use conjunctions in a variety of contexts for effective oral and written communication
d) realise the importance of conjunctions in communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Coordinating conjunctions

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why do we join sentences?
2. Which words do we use to join sentences?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This competence are realised as the learner engages in assigned activities collaboratively.
• Digital Literacy: This is enhanced as the learner interacts with technology while typing their sentences on a digital device.

## Values
• Responsibility: It is seen as the learner engages in assigned roles and duties in different activities while learning conjunctions.
• Unity: This is achieved as the learner shares the available resources like the digital devices so that peers can as well type their sentences on the device.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Personal Hygiene: This is promoted as the learner listens to short dialogues on sanitation and how to take care of oneself.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner relates the knowledge on conjunctions to similar concepts taught in Kiswahili.
• The learner relates content learnt from the theme of hygiene and sanitation to what is learnt in Agriculture and Creative Arts.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 10.0 Hygiene and Sanitation, Sub-strand 10.3.1 Grammar in Use: Conjunctions

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Finding coordinating conjunctions

LESSON 1: FINDING COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS
===========================================

## What you will learn
• Name the seven coordinating conjunctions.
• Find them in sentences about hygiene and sanitation.
• Say why joining words make speech clearer.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify conjunctions correctly in oral and written texts for fluency in speech; d) realise the importance of conjunctions in communication

## Introduction
Read these two lines aloud. 'I wash my hands. I rinse them.' Now read this one. 'I wash my hands and I rinse them.' The second line sounds smoother because one small word joins the two actions.

## Notes
### What a conjunction does
A conjunction is a word that joins. It can join two words, two groups of words or two sentences. When ideas are joined, a listener does not have to guess how they fit. The speech flows.

### Coordinating conjunctions
Coordinating conjunctions join parts that are equal in importance. There are seven of them. A useful memory word is FANBOYS:

- for — gives a reason, like because
- and — adds another idea
- nor — adds a second negative idea
- but — shows a difference
- or — shows a choice
- yet — shows a difference that surprises us
- so — shows a result

### Find them in this text
We sweep the classroom and we mop the floor. The bin is full, so we empty it. Use a broom or a mop, but do not leave the floor wet. The soap is small, yet it still cleans our hands. We cover the food, for flies spread germs. I do not touch refuse with bare hands, nor do I forget to wash.

The joining words in that text are and, so, or, but, yet, for and nor. Each one tells the listener a different relationship. And adds. So gives a result. Or offers a choice. But and yet show a difference. For gives a reason. Nor continues a negative idea.

### Why they matter
Without conjunctions, talk sounds like a list of separate pieces. With them, a listener hears whether you are adding, choosing, contrasting or explaining. That is why conjunctions help fluency. You say more in a sentence, and the meaning stays clear.

## Key words
• conjunction — a word that joins words, groups of words or sentences
• coordinating conjunction — a joining word that links equal ideas, such as and, but or so
• fluency — speaking or writing that flows smoothly and is easy to follow

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which word is the conjunction, and what job does it do? The latrine was dirty, so we scrubbed it.

Working:
1. Find the word that joins the two ideas.
2. Ask what relationship it shows: adding, choice, difference, reason or result.

Answer: So. It shows the result of the latrine being dirty.

### Example 2
Name the conjunction in this sentence: Wash with soap or rinse every part of your hands with clean water.

Working:
1. The sentence offers two ways to act.
2. The word between the two ways is the conjunction.

Answer: Or. It shows a choice.

## Activity: Hunt the joining words
You will need: The short hygiene text in the notes, A pencil, Exercise book
1. In pairs, read the hygiene text aloud, taking one sentence each.
2. Underline every coordinating conjunction.
3. Beside each one, write its job: add, choice, difference, reason or result.
4. Ask your partner one question that uses a conjunction, for example: Do you sweep or mop first?
5. Answer in a full sentence that keeps the same conjunction.

## Practice
1. List the seven coordinating conjunctions.
2. What is the conjunction, and what does it show? The soap is small, yet it cleans well.
3. Why do we join sentences?

## Summary
• A conjunction joins ideas.
• The coordinating conjunctions are for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so.
• Each one shows a different link, such as adding, choosing or giving a result.

### Answers to practice
1. for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
2. Yet. It shows a surprising difference.
3. So that ideas flow and the listener can tell how the ideas fit together.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Conjunctions in a short dialogue

LESSON 2: CONJUNCTIONS IN A SHORT DIALOGUE
==========================================

## What you will learn
• Hear conjunctions in a spoken dialogue about sanitation.
• Say short dialogues that use them naturally.
• Ask and answer questions that contain conjunctions.

Curriculum outcomes: b) engage in short dialogues featuring conjunctions for fluency in speech; c) use conjunctions in a variety of contexts for effective oral and written communication

## Introduction
When two people talk about cleaning, they do not speak in single short bursts. They add ideas, give reasons and show results. Listen for the small words that do that work.

## Notes
### A dialogue to listen to
Asha and Juma are on toilet duty.

Asha: The floor is wet and it smells bad, so we should scrub it.
Juma: I have a broom and a mop, but I have no disinfectant.
Asha: We can use soap or clean water with a scrubbing brush.
Juma: I am tired, yet I will stay and help.
Asha: I will fetch a bucket, for the tank is full.
Juma: I will not leave the work to you, nor will I forget to wash my hands afterwards.

### Talk about how they are used
And joins two facts: the floor is wet and it smells. So gives the result: they should scrub it. But shows a problem that stands against Juma's tools: he has a broom and a mop, but no disinfectant. Or gives Asha's choice of cleaners. Yet shows that Juma helps even though he is tired. For gives Asha's reason for fetching water. Nor adds a second thing Juma will not do.

Notice the pattern after nor. We say 'nor will I forget', not 'nor I will forget'. The helping verb comes before I.

### Speaking them yourself
A good dialogue has a reason to talk. Here the reason is keeping the toilet safe. When you speak, do not drop the conjunction. 'I have a broom. I have no soap.' is correct but choppy. 'I have a broom, but I have no soap.' tells your partner the contrast at once.

Put a comma before but, yet, so, for and nor when they join two full sentences. You do not need a comma in a short pair such as 'soap and water' or 'a broom or a mop'.

### Questions that use conjunctions
Do you flush the toilet and wash your hands?
Is the latrine dirty or clean?
The floor is wet, so what should we do?
Answer in a full sentence so that the conjunction stays in the reply.

## Key words
• dialogue — a conversation between two or more people
• contrast — a clear difference between two ideas
• disinfectant — a liquid used to kill germs on surfaces

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Juma says, 'I am tired, yet I will stay and help.' Which two conjunctions does he use, and what does each one do?

Working:
1. Find both joining words.
2. Yet joins the two sentences. And joins stay and help.

Answer: Yet shows a surprising difference. And adds the second action, help.

### Example 2
Join these two ideas in speech: We cover the food. Flies carry germs.

Working:
1. The second idea is the reason for the first.
2. Use for or so, depending on the order.

Answer: We cover the food, for flies carry germs. Or: Flies carry germs, so we cover the food.

## Activity: Sanitation dialogue
You will need: The dialogue in the notes, Exercise books
1. Listen as two learners read the dialogue aloud. The class notes every conjunction they hear.
2. In pairs, discuss what each conjunction does in the line where it appears.
3. Change two lines so that they are about washing hands, but keep a conjunction in each new line.
4. Perform your short dialogue for another pair and ask them one question that uses or or and.

## Practice
1. Complete with a suitable conjunction: The bin is full, ______ we should empty it.
2. Rewrite as one sentence: I swept the floor. I did not mop it.
3. Ask a question about handwashing that uses or.
4. What is wrong with this sentence, and how would you say it? I do not litter, nor I waste water.

## Summary
• Dialogues use conjunctions to add, contrast, choose, explain and show results.
• After nor, use the order nor + helping verb + subject.
• A comma often comes before but, yet, so, for and nor when they join two sentences.

### Answers to practice
1. so
2. I swept the floor, but I did not mop it.
3. Example: Do you wash your hands with soap or with water only?
4. After nor, the helping verb comes first: I do not litter, nor do I waste water.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Using conjunctions in your own sentences

LESSON 3: USING CONJUNCTIONS IN YOUR OWN SENTENCES
==================================================

## What you will learn
• Build correct sentences with each coordinating conjunction.
• Choose the conjunction that matches the meaning.
• Explain how conjunctions help oral and written communication.

Curriculum outcomes: c) use conjunctions in a variety of contexts for effective oral and written communication; d) realise the importance of conjunctions in communication

## Introduction
Choosing the wrong joining word changes the message. 'The water is dirty, so we drink it' says the opposite of what you mean. The small word has to match the idea.

## Notes
### Match the word to the meaning
Before you join two ideas, decide the link.

- Add: Wash your hands and dry them.
- Choice: Boil the water or treat it.
- Difference: The toilet is old, but it is clean.
- Surprising difference: She was late, yet she still swept the room.
- Result: The drain was blocked, so dirty water collected.
- Reason: He wore shoes in the latrine, for the floor was wet.
- Second negative: She does not leave food uncovered, nor does she drink unsafe water.

If you are not sure between but and yet, remember that both show difference. Yet adds the feeling that the second idea is unexpected. If you are not sure between so and for, check the order. So follows the cause: cause, so result. For follows the result: result, for cause.

### Building a sentence
Start with two short sentences. 'The broom is broken. We cannot sweep.' The second sentence is the result, so join them: 'The broom is broken, so we cannot sweep.'

Check three things. Does the conjunction show the link you want? Are both sides complete thoughts when you use but, yet, so, for or nor? Did you keep the meaning true? 'We have no soap, so we leave our hands dirty' may be what someone does, but it is not the safe choice. A better sentence is 'We have no soap, so we ask for some before we eat.'

### In writing and in speech
In speech, conjunctions stop you from pausing awkwardly between ideas. In writing, they build longer sentences that a reader can follow. A paragraph about hygiene becomes clearer when each sentence shows how the next action follows.

Conjunctions do not decorate a sentence. They carry meaning. Using the right one is part of communicating well, at home, in class and whenever you explain how to stay healthy.

## Key words
• result — what happens because of something else
• reason — why something is done
• negative — a sentence or idea that says no or not

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Choose for, so or but: We rinse the cups, ______ soap left on them can make a drink taste bad.

Working:
1. The second part gives the reason for rinsing.
2. Reason after the action uses for.

Answer: for

### Example 2
Join without changing the meaning: Otieno does not throw rubbish in the drain. He does not block the toilet with plastic.

Working:
1. Both ideas are negative.
2. Use nor, and put the helping verb before the subject.

Answer: Otieno does not throw rubbish in the drain, nor does he block the toilet with plastic.

## Activity: Type the seven links
You will need: Exercise book, A phone, tablet or computer if one is available to share
1. Each learner writes seven sentences about hygiene, one for each conjunction: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
2. Swap books and check that the conjunction matches the meaning.
3. Correct any sentence that uses the wrong link.
4. If a digital device is available, take turns to type two of your best sentences and read them aloud to the group.

## Practice
1. Join with so: The latrine has no lid. Flies go in and out.
2. Join with but: The compound is swept every day. The toilet is still dirty.
3. Which conjunction fits? Keep the food covered, ______ dust will fall into it. (for / yet / or)
4. Give one reason conjunctions are important in communication.

## Summary
• Choose the conjunction that matches the link you mean.
• So follows a cause. For follows a result and gives the reason.
• The right conjunction keeps both speech and writing clear.

### Answers to practice
1. The latrine has no lid, so flies go in and out.
2. The compound is swept every day, but the toilet is still dirty.
3. for
4. They show how ideas are linked, so the listener or reader understands the meaning clearly.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 10.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: WORD CLASS (CONJUNCTIONS)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word is a coordinating conjunction?
   A. quickly
   B. because
   C. but
   D. under

2. In 'Sweep the floor and mop it', what does and do?
   A. Shows a choice
   B. Adds another action
   C. Gives a reason
   D. Shows a result

3. Which conjunction shows a result?
   A. or
   B. so
   C. yet
   D. nor

4. Choose the correct sentence.
   A. I do not waste water, nor I leave the tap running.
   B. I do not waste water, nor do I leave the tap running.
   C. I do not waste water, nor does leave the tap running.
   D. I do not waste water nor do leave the tap running.

5. Asha says, 'I have a mop, but I have no soap.' The conjunction but shows
   A. a result
   B. a choice
   C. a difference
   D. a reason

6. Which question uses a conjunction correctly?
   A. Do you flush or cover the latrine?
   B. Do you flush cover the latrine?
   C. Flush you or cover?
   D. Do flush and you cover?

7. The drain is blocked, ______ dirty water stays in the yard. Which word fits?
   A. or
   B. so
   C. yet
   D. nor

8. We boil the water, for it may be unsafe. What does for mean here?
   A. and also
   B. as a choice
   C. because
   D. instead

9. Why are conjunctions important in communication?

10. Which pair is joined in the most suitable way?
   A. The soap fell in the drain, so we fished it out.
   B. The soap fell in the drain, or we fished it out.
   C. The soap fell in the drain, nor we fished it out.
   D. The soap fell in the drain, for we fished it out.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 10.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: WORD CLASS (CONJUNCTIONS)
========================================

1. C. but
   But is one of the seven coordinating conjunctions. Because is a joining word too, but it is not in this FANBOYS set.

2. B. Adds another action
   And adds the second action to the first.

3. B. so
   So introduces what happens because of the first idea.

4. B. I do not waste water, nor do I leave the tap running.
   After nor, the helping verb comes before the subject: nor do I.

5. C. a difference
   But contrasts having a mop with having no soap.

6. A. Do you flush or cover the latrine?
   Or joins the two choices inside a proper question.

7. B. so
   Dirty water staying there is the result of the blocked drain.

8. C. because
   For gives the reason, in the same way because does.

9. They join ideas and show the link between them, so speech and writing are clear and fluent.
   Conjunctions carry meaning; they are not extra decoration.

10. A. The soap fell in the drain, so we fished it out.
   Fishing it out is the result, so so is the right link.

LESSON 3: USING CONJUNCTIONS IN YOUR OWN SENTENCES
==================================================

• Choose the conjunction that matches the meaning.

### In writing and in speech
In speech, conjunctions stop you from pausing awkwardly between ideas. In writing, they build longer sentences that a reader can follow. A paragraph about hygiene becomes clearer when each sentence shows how the next action follows.

Conjunctions do not decorate a sentence. They carry meaning. Using the right one is part of communicating well, at home, in class and whenever you explain how to stay healthy.

## Key words
• result — what happens because of something else
• reason — why something is done
• negative — a sentence or idea that says no or not

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Choose for, so or but: We rinse the cups, ______ soap left on them can make a drink taste bad.

Working:
1. The second part gives the reason for rinsing.
2. Reason after the action uses for.

Answer: for

### Example 2
Join without changing the meaning: Otieno does not throw rubbish in the drain. He does not block the toilet with plastic.

Working:
1. Both ideas are negative.
2. Use nor, and put the helping verb before the subject.

Answer: Otieno does not throw rubbish in the drain, nor does he block the toilet with plastic.

## Activity: Type the seven links
You will need: Exercise book, A phone, tablet or computer if one is available to share
1. Each learner writes seven sentences about hygiene, one for each conjunction: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
2. Swap books and check that the conjunction matches the meaning.
3. Correct any sentence that uses the wrong link.
4. If a digital device is available, take turns to type two of your best sentences and read them aloud to the group.

## Practice
1. Join with so: The latrine has no lid. Flies go in and out.
2. Join with but: The compound is swept every day. The toilet is still dirty.
3. Which conjunction fits? Keep the food covered, ______ dust will fall into it. (for / yet / or)
4. Give one reason conjunctions are important in communication.

## Summary
• Choose the conjunction that matches the link you mean.
• So follows a cause. For follows a result and gives the reason.
• The right conjunction keeps both speech and writing clear.

### Answers to practice
1. The latrine has no lid, so flies go in and out.
2. The compound is swept every day, but the toilet is still dirty.
3. for
4. They show how ideas are linked, so the listener or reader understands the meaning clearly.

questions.question: Which word is a coordinating conjunction?
questions.explanation: But is one of the seven coordinating conjunctions. Because is a joining word too, but it is not in this FANBOYS set.

questions.question: In 'Sweep the floor and mop it', what does and do?
questions.explanation: And adds the second action to the first.

questions.question: Which conjunction shows a result?
questions.explanation: So introduces what happens because of the first idea.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I do not waste water, nor I leave the tap running.
I do not waste water, nor do I leave the tap running.
I do not waste water, nor does leave the tap running.
I do not waste water nor do leave the tap running.
questions.explanation: After nor, the helping verb comes before the subject: nor do I.

questions.question: Asha says, 'I have a mop, but I have no soap.' The conjunction but shows
questions.explanation: But contrasts having a mop with having no soap.

questions.question: Which question uses a conjunction correctly?
options: Do you flush or cover the latrine?
Do you flush cover the latrine?
questions.explanation: Or joins the two choices inside a proper question.

questions.question: The drain is blocked, ______ dirty water stays in the yard. Which word fits?
questions.explanation: Dirty water staying there is the result of the blocked drain.

questions.question: We boil the water, for it may be unsafe. What does for mean here?
questions.explanation: For gives the reason, in the same way because does.

questions.question: Why are conjunctions important in communication?
questions.answer: They join ideas and show the link between them, so speech and writing are clear and fluent.
questions.explanation: Conjunctions carry meaning; they are not extra decoration.

questions.question: Which pair is joined in the most suitable way?
options: The soap fell in the drain, so we fished it out.
The soap fell in the drain, or we fished it out.
The soap fell in the drain, nor we fished it out.
The soap fell in the drain, for we fished it out.
questions.explanation: Fishing it out is the result, so so is the right link.
